own_scenes.desc: Los grupos de Tamla/Motown ocuparon el hueco de los girl groups: Martha and the Vandellas («Heat Wave», «Dancing in the Street», «Nowhere to Run»), Gladys Knight, las Marvelettes, las Velvelettes y, sobre todo, las Supremes, el grupo pop americano de más éxito del momento (seis números 1 en dos años). Tres amigas del proyecto Brewster-Douglass, las «Supremes sin éxitos» hasta «Where Did Our Love Go» (1964): Berry Gordy vio en ellas el caballo de Troya para entrar en el mercado blanco, con los Funk Brothers, la escritura «psicológica» de Holland-Dozier-Holland (playlets femeninos sobre el amor como adicción, música dura contra letras sumisas) y el departamento de Artist Development de Maxine Powell y Cholly Atkins. Su imagen de espectáculo (Copacabana, pelucas) contrastaba con la nueva bohemia rock, como en su incómodo encuentro con unos Beatles fumados. Diana Ross ardía: seis números 1 y aún las trataban como a un grupo cualquiera.

notes.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo
notes.text: En 1964 Billboard dejó de publicar la lista de R&B, señal de integración; «Dancing in the Street» de Martha and the Vandellas, una llamada a las armas, llegó al número 2. El 27 de diciembre las Supremes entraron en millones de hogares desde el Ed Sullivan Show. En 1965 Motown fue el primer vendedor de singles del país y en 1966 sumaría veintidós Top 10: una cadena de montaje como la de Ford, canciones con ganchos repetidos que atrapaban en un bucle y un sonido de bajo y tambor-pandereta ideal para conducir. Ric-Tic, con músicos de Motown pluriempleados, lanzó «Agent Double-O-Soul» de Edwin Starr. Gordy mantenía la política fuera de Motown, para frustración de Marvin Gaye tras Watts; Malcolm X premió a Motown en Detroit una semana antes de morir. En julio de 1966 Stevie Wonder rompió la regla con su versión de «Blowin’ in the Wind», número 9 en septiembre.

notes.chapter: Octubre: Winchester Cathedral: tiempo pasado, presente y futuro
notes.text: El 1 de octubre había tres discos de Motown en el Top 10 americano: «You Can’t Hurry Love», «Beauty Is Only Skin Deep» y «Reach Out I’ll Be There»; una edad de oro que no se reflejaba en la política ni en la vida de los negros. Canciones como «Reach Out» ofrecían apoyo a comunidades bajo enorme presión. A mediados de mes salió «You Keep Me Hangin’ On» de las Supremes, con guitarras como un telégrafo y una dureza que recuerda más que la sumisión.

notes.chapter: Noviembre: Good Vibrations: Motown y el soul en Reino Unido, los Beach Boys y el Sunset Strip
notes.text: En julio Berry Gordy ordenó no publicar nada que no fuera Top 10, y en las Supremes solo números 1: «You Can’t Hurry Love» y «Reach Out I’ll Be There» lo cumplieron. KRLA Beat anunció 1966 como «el año del sonido Motown».

refs.q: Much of the slack created by the demise of the girl groups had been taken up by the Tamla/Motown artists.
refs.para: Much of the slack created by the demise of the girl groups had been taken up by the Tamla/Motown artists. Berry Gordy had a roster of powerful female vocalists and groups in the mid-sixties: Gladys Knight and the Pips, the Marvellettes, the Velvelettes, Brenda Holloway, and Martha and the Vandellas, whose tough, soaring, surging 1963–5 Top 10 hits – ‘Heat Wave’, ‘Quicksand’, ‘Dancing in the Street’, ‘Nowhere to Run’ – remain without peer. But the biggest of them all – and the most successful American pop group of the period – were the Supremes. By May 1966, they had racked up eight Top 20 hits, including six #1s, in just under two years – an astonishing achievement. Their latest record was ‘Love Is Like an Itching in My Heart’, a fairly straightforward lyrical riff on the idea of a ‘love bug’ set to the usual compulsively propulsive Motown template. By mid-month, it was in the Top 20.
refs.chapter: Mayo: Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog: la mística de la feminidad y la independencia femenina

refs.q: Gordy saw something more malleable in the Supremes: they would be the Trojan Horse for Motown’s assimilation into the white mainstream.
refs.para: Motown had already tasted significant pop success with the Miracles, the Marvelettes and Mary Wells, but Gordy saw something more malleable in the Supremes: they would be the Trojan Horse for Motown’s assimilation into the white mainstream. The team was there: the musicians, the Funk Brothers; the writers, Holland–Dozier–Holland; and now the group. The Supremes would become a hit machine, and ‘Where Did Our Love Go?’ was the template.
refs.chapter: Mayo: Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog: la mística de la feminidad y la independencia femenina

refs.q: In contrast, Diana Ross was a scorch of anger and pride
refs.para: In contrast, Diana Ross was a scorch of anger and pride: ‘We’ve had six number-one hits in a row, but we’re still treated like some ordinary rock ’n’ roll group. On TV shows like Ed Sullivan’s, we’re pushed on and off the stage fast, as if we were nothin’, and there are the Supremes, cryin’ behind the wings … I see all these phonies who never even had one number-one hit runnin’ around actin’ like big stars. I’ve got something they don’t have, and the kids know it.’
refs.chapter: Mayo: Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog: la mística de la feminidad y la independencia femenina

refs.q: Reflecting Detroit’s core industry and Gordy’s own working experience at the Lincoln-Mercury plant, Motown was run on the basis of an auto assembly line
refs.para: Berry Gordy’s integrationist policy was working, with huge hits in both the pop and the R&B charts. Reflecting Detroit’s core industry and Gordy’s own working experience at the Lincoln-Mercury plant, Motown was run on the basis of an auto assembly line: songs were often constructed out of interchangeable parts, to be assembled at a later date and assigned to whichever artist Gordy and his team felt would suit.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: Releasing this record was a deliberate statement on Wonder’s part
refs.para: Releasing this record was a deliberate statement on Wonder’s part, the first time that a Motown artist had broken Gordy’s ‘no politics’ rule. In another metaphorical comment on the state of the civil rights movement, its message was hopeful, yet realistic and resigned: the battle was far from being won, but if we stand together, we might still reach the mountain top.
refs.chapter: Julio: Land of 1000 Dances: Tamla, el soul y la Marcha contra el Miedo

refs.q: This was some kind of golden age, but the optimism and strength of these records was not reflected in black politics or black lives.
refs.para: This was some kind of golden age, but the optimism and strength of these records was not reflected in black politics or black lives. The civil rights movement had shaped and seen itself reflected in the records that Motown and Stax put into the mainstream. Quite apart from consciousness-raising efforts like Brenda Holloway’s August single, ‘Play It Cool, Stay in School’, the lyrics of songs like Stevie Wonder’s cover of ‘Blowin’ in the Wind’ or ‘Reach Out I’ll Be There’ offered advice and sustenance to communities and politicians under extreme duress.
refs.chapter: Octubre: Winchester Cathedral: tiempo pasado, presente y futuro

refs.q: 1966 will undoubtedly be recorded as “The Year Of The Motown Sound” in pop history
refs.para: The first demand might have been impossible, but ‘You Can’t Hurry Love’ went to #1 in the US in September. ‘Reach Out I’ll Be There’ then hit the top. In early November, as ‘You Keep Me Hangin’ On’ was waiting in the wings, KRLA Beat noted what seemed like a conveyor belt: ‘1966 will undoubtedly be recorded as “The Year Of The Motown Sound” in pop history, as one after another of the Motown groups takes up residence in the Number One spot in the charts.’

podcast.title: Blueprint for PIR
podcast.body: Motown served as the explicit and foundational blueprint for Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff when they embarked on creating their own record label, Philadelphia International Records, inspiring their business and creative model. "Motown was their blueprint."

podcast.title: Crossover Appeal Strategy
podcast.body: Motown effectively attracted a white audience by skillfully incorporating familiar pop elements into its music, while simultaneously retaining its African American following through its R&B roots and subtle gospel influences, thereby achieving broad mass appeal. "Motel was able to draw a white audience for its music because the songs had these familiar pop elements, but it also maintained its African American following because the songs were still R&B with the times a little tinge of gospel."

podcast.title: Local Musicians for Live Gigs – Iggy Pop's Role
podcast.body: In the mid-sixties, many Motown acts such as The Shangri-La's, The Temptations, and The Four Tops toured with only a couple of core musicians (typically a guitar and piano player). They would then hire local musicians, including bass players and drummers, to fill out the live band, rehearsing briefly before each show. Iggy Pop was one such local drummer, highly skilled at picking up songs quickly. "When a lot of the Motown acts at the time You know the Shangri-La's and the temptations and the four tops and others played live gigs They toured just with a couple of musicians usually guitar player and maybe a piano player The rest of the band including the bass player and the drummer would be hired locally."

podcast.title: Relaxed Rhythms
podcast.body: Motown music is characterized by its "relaxed rhythms," which can influence drummers like Chad Smith and contribute to their playing style. "Chad Smith, a big hard-hitting dude from Detroit who grew up listening to the relaxed rhythms of Motown."

podcast.title: Resistance to Political Messages
podcast.body: Berry Gordy, the founder and president of Motown, was strongly opposed to the inclusion of overt political messages in Motown songs, famously resisting Marvin Gaye's desire to release "What's Going On." "Barry Gordy, whose Motowns founder and president was also very resistant to political messages in Motown songs."
